a2z.a2z-1-1: The goal here isn't syntax memorization — it's getting comfortable enough with your language that you stop thinking about it while solving problems. If I/O, loops, and functions still take conscious effort, everything after this step will feel harder than it needs to.
a2z.a2z-1-2: Pattern problems exist purely to train nested-loop thinking: figure out how the row and column indices relate to what gets printed. Once that clicks here, spotting the same row/column relationships inside real array and matrix problems gets much easier.
a2z.a2z-1-3: Knowing what your language's standard library already gives you (sorting, sets, maps, heaps) saves you from reinventing them mid-interview. You don't need to memorize every method — just know what exists so you reach for it instead of hand-rolling it.
a2z.a2z-1-4: A handful of math ideas — divisors, primality, GCD, basic combinatorics — resurface constantly in DP and array problems as small subroutines. Learn them once here so you're not derailed by “wait, how do I even find divisors” mid-problem later.
a2z.a2z-1-5: Every recursive solution boils down to a base case and a recurrence — the hard part is trusting the recursive call to solve the smaller subproblem instead of trying to trace the whole call stack in your head. Draw the recursion tree for a couple of these until that trust is automatic.
a2z.a2z-1-6: Precomputing frequencies or presence in a hash map turns an O(n²) nested-loop search into O(n). If your instinct on a problem is “loop through and check”, pause and ask whether a map removes the inner loop entirely.
a2z.a2z-2-1: Selection, bubble, and insertion sort aren't things you'll hand-code in an interview — they're here so you internalize what O(n²) actually looks like and can reason about stability and in-place swaps.
a2z.a2z-2-2: Merge sort and quicksort are the sorts that actually matter: merge sort for its guaranteed O(n log n) and quicksort for its in-place partitioning trick, which reappears directly in the 'kth largest' quickselect pattern later.
a2z.a2z-3-1: Two pointers and single-pass scans dominate this tier — most “easy” array problems are really asking whether you can avoid a nested loop by tracking one running value as you go.
a2z.a2z-3-2: This is where Kadane's algorithm, next permutation, and the Dutch national flag (sort 0/1/2) partition trick live — three patterns worth truly internalizing, since variations of each show up constantly on other sheets.
a2z.a2z-3-3: Merge-sort-based counting (inversions, reverse pairs) is the throughline here: once you see how merging two sorted halves lets you count cross-pairs for free, several “hard” array problems stop looking hard.
a2z.a2z-4-1: Binary search isn't just 'find x in a sorted array' — lower/upper bound and the rotated-array variants are about carefully redefining what 'sorted' and 'target' mean for each problem while keeping the same halving logic.
a2z.a2z-4-2: “Binary search on the answer” is the real unlock: when a problem asks for a minimum/maximum value satisfying some condition, and that condition is monotonic, you can binary search over the answer space itself instead of the input array.
a2z.a2z-4-3: Treating a 2D grid as a flattened 1D array (via row/col math) lets every 1D binary search technique apply directly — the row-wise-sorted-matrix problems are the best test of whether that mental mapping is solid.
a2z.a2z-5-1: String problems are mostly array problems wearing a costume — frequency counting, two pointers, and prefix comparisons all carry over directly once you stop treating strings as a special case.
a2z.a2z-5-2: These lean on hashing and careful index bookkeeping (substring counting, beauty-of-substrings) rather than new theory — the difficulty is precision, not novelty.
a2z.a2z-6-1: Get comfortable with dummy-head nodes and drawing the pointer rewiring on paper before coding it — almost every linked-list bug is an off-by-one in 'next' reassignment, not a logic error.
a2z.a2z-6-2: Doubly-linked lists add a prev pointer to keep in sync on every insert/delete — the extra bookkeeping is the whole point, since it trades that complexity for O(1) removal given just a node reference.
a2z.a2z-6-3: Fast-and-slow (tortoise/hare) pointers solve most of this tier: middle-of-list, cycle detection, and palindrome-checking are all the same two-pointer idea aimed at slightly different questions.
a2z.a2z-6-4: Same fast/slow toolkit as singly linked lists, just with the added ability to walk backward — use that when a problem would otherwise need extra bookkeeping to find a previous node.
a2z.a2z-6-5: Reversal-in-groups and merging k lists both come down to 'can you manipulate raw pointers without losing a reference' — do these on paper first, since debugging pointer logic mentally is much harder than debugging it on a whiteboard.
a2z.a2z-7-1: Before optimizing anything, get used to writing the recurrence relation directly from the problem statement — pow(x, n) and counting “good numbers” are really about spotting repeated substructure, not about recursion syntax.
a2z.a2z-7-2: The 'pick or don't pick' template (include this element in the subsequence, or skip it) solves the entire subset/subsequence family — learn that one recursive skeleton and combination-sum-style problems become variations on a theme.
a2z.a2z-7-3: Backtracking is 'pick or don't pick' plus explicit undo: try a choice, recurse, then revert it before trying the next one. N-Queens and Sudoku are the clearest place to see why that undo step matters.
a2z.a2z-8-1: Bit tricks (AND/OR/XOR/shifts) look arcane until you see them as compact ways to represent sets and toggles — once that clicks, checking/setting/clearing a bit is just arithmetic on that representation.
a2z.a2z-8-2: XOR's cancel-itself-out property is the single idea behind most of these — 'find the element that appears once' and its variants are all disguises for the same XOR trick.
a2z.a2z-8-3: Fast exponentiation (binary exponentiation) reuses the same halving idea as binary search and merge sort — repeatedly squaring instead of multiplying one step at a time turns O(n) into O(log n).
a2z.a2z-9-1: Array, linked-list, and two-queue implementations of a stack/queue all exist to make one thing concrete: these are interfaces (push/pop, enqueue/dequeue), not specific data structures — you can build them from almost anything.
a2z.a2z-9-2: Pick one method (usually two-stack) for infix-to-postfix-to-prefix conversion and understand it deeply rather than memorizing all six directions — they're all the same operator-precedence idea run in different orders.
a2z.a2z-9-3: The monotonic stack pattern (keep the stack increasing or decreasing, pop when the new element breaks that order) is the highest-leverage idea in this whole sheet — next-greater-element, histogram area, and trapping rainwater are all this one trick.
a2z.a2z-9-4: LRU/LFU cache problems test whether you can combine a hash map (O(1) lookup) with a doubly-linked list (O(1) reordering) — the map alone or the list alone can't hit the required time complexity, only the pair together.
a2z.a2z-10-1: Variable-size sliding window (grow the window, shrink it when a condition breaks) replaces a nested loop with two pointers moving forward only — that “each pointer moves at most n times” observation is what gives it O(n).
a2z.a2z-10-2: The hard tier is the same variable-window idea applied to trickier shrink conditions (at-most-k-distinct, exactly-k-distinct via at-most-k minus at-most-(k-1)) — the window mechanics don't change, only what you're counting inside it.
a2z.a2z-11-1: A heap is just a complete binary tree stored in an array where every parent beats its children — internalize the array-index math (2i+1, 2i+2, (i-1)/2) once and 'implement a heap' stops being intimidating.
a2z.a2z-11-2: Most “medium” heap problems are really “maintain the k best elements seen so far” — a fixed-size heap that evicts its worst element on overflow is the recurring shape.
a2z.a2z-11-3: Two-heap designs (a max-heap for the lower half, a min-heap for the upper half) are how you get the running median or similar order-statistics in better than O(n) per query — the split-in-half idea generalizes further than it first appears.
a2z.a2z-12-1: Greedy works when the locally-best choice is provably never worse than any other choice long-term — these easy problems (activity selection, lemonade change) are good for building the instinct for when that's actually true.
a2z.a2z-12-2: Interval-scheduling and job-sequencing problems are where greedy's proof matters most — sorting by the right key (end time, deadline, ratio) is usually the entire solution once you've identified it.
a2z.a2z-13-1: DFS (pre/in/post-order) and BFS (level-order) traversals are the vocabulary every later tree problem is written in — the iterative versions using an explicit stack are worth doing once so recursion doesn't feel mandatory.
a2z.a2z-13-2: Most medium tree problems are a traversal with extra bookkeeping carried along (a running max, a path list, a boolean flag) — identify which traversal fits, then figure out what extra state needs to travel with it.
a2z.a2z-13-3: Path-sum and diameter problems need a function that returns one value up to its parent while separately updating a global/outer answer — that “return vs. update global” split is the key insight worth isolating.
a2z.a2z-14-1: A BST's core guarantee (left < node < right) is what makes search, insert, and delete O(log n) on a balanced tree — deletion is the fiddly one, since removing a node with two children means promoting its in-order successor.
a2z.a2z-14-2: In-order traversal of a BST always yields sorted order — that single fact solves validation, kth-smallest, and successor/predecessor problems almost immediately once you reach for it.
a2z.a2z-15-1: Adjacency lists (not matrices) are the default representation for anything but a dense graph — get comfortable building one from an edge list before touching any traversal algorithm.
a2z.a2z-15-2: BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs; DFS is simpler for existence/connectivity questions (does a path exist, is this a valid cycle). Most 'flood fill' style grid problems are BFS/DFS on an implicit graph where cells are nodes.
a2z.a2z-15-3: Topological sort only exists for DAGs, and it's really 'process nodes only after all their prerequisites are processed' — Kahn's algorithm (BFS with in-degree counting) makes that requirement mechanical instead of implicit.
a2z.a2z-15-4: Dijkstra's is BFS with a priority queue standing in for a plain queue, so it expands the currently-cheapest node first — that's the whole conceptual leap from unweighted to non-negative-weighted shortest paths. Bellman-Ford and Floyd-Warshall handle the cases Dijkstra can't: negative edges and all-pairs.
a2z.a2z-15-5: Union-Find (with path compression + union by rank) turns 'are these two nodes connected' into a near-O(1) check, which is exactly what Kruskal's MST algorithm and dynamic-connectivity problems need.
a2z.a2z-15-6: Tarjan's algorithm for bridges/articulation points and Kosaraju's for strongly connected components both hinge on discovery-time and low-link values tracked during a single DFS pass — the bookkeeping is the hard part, not the traversal itself.
a2z.a2z-16-1: DP is recursion plus “stop recomputing the same subproblem” — memoization (top-down) and tabulation (bottom-up) are the same recurrence, just written in opposite directions. Get one recursive brute force working first; the DP optimization comes after.
a2z.a2z-16-2: Frog Jump and House Robber establish the template for the rest of the sheet: define what state a 1D index represents, write the recurrence in terms of smaller indices, then space-optimize from an array down to two variables.
a2z.a2z-16-3: Grid DP just adds a second dimension to the same idea — each cell's answer depends on the cell(s) that can reach it (usually above and left). Ninja's Training's 3D state (index, day, last-task) is worth studying closely since 3D DP recurs later.
a2z.a2z-16-4: The 'pick or don't pick' recursion from Step 7 becomes a DP the moment you memoize it — subset-sum, partition, and target-sum are all that same recursion with a different question asked of the final states.
a2z.a2z-16-5: Two-string DP problems (LCS, edit distance) use a 2D table indexed by (position in string A, position in string B) — draw the table by hand for a tiny example once, and every problem in this group becomes a variation of the same grid.
a2z.a2z-16-6: Every 'buy and sell stock' variant is the same state machine (holding a stock or not, possibly with cooldown/fee/transaction-count limits) — identify what extra dimension the variant adds to that base state.
a2z.a2z-16-7: The O(n²) longest-increasing-subsequence DP is intuitive but the O(n log n) patience-sorting version (binary search on a tails array) is what actually gets asked for in interviews — learn both, since the second only makes sense once you understand the first.
a2z.a2z-16-8: Matrix Chain Multiplication's 'try every split point' recursion is the template for interval DP — Burst Balloons and Palindrome Partitioning both reduce to picking where to split the range and recursing on both sides.
a2z.a2z-16-9: These are 2D DP where the state represents “the largest valid square/rectangle ending at this cell” — the recurrence usually looks at the min of three neighbors, which is worth memorizing as its own small pattern.
a2z.a2z-17-1: A trie is a tree where each edge is a character, so any string's presence or prefix status is just a walk down the tree — the insert/search/startsWith trio is the whole data structure.
a2z.a2z-17-2: Tries excel whenever the question is 'about prefixes' or 'about many strings sharing structure' — a bitwise trie (one bit per level instead of one character) unlocks the maximum-XOR-pair family of problems the same way.
a2z.a2z-18-1: Rabin-Karp (rolling hash) and KMP (the prefix/failure function) are two different ways to avoid re-scanning the string on every mismatch during substring search — worth knowing both exist even if you only fully internalize one.

neetcode.Arrays & Hashing: Hash maps turn “have I seen this before” from an O(n) scan into an O(1) lookup — most problems here are testing whether that's your first instinct, not whether you know a clever trick.
neetcode.Two Pointers: Two pointers work whenever moving one side forward can only help and moving it backward would only make things worse — that monotonic guarantee is what lets you drop a nested loop down to O(n).
neetcode.Sliding Window: A window that only expands and contracts (never resets) is what keeps this pattern linear — the moment you find yourself restarting the window from scratch, you've left O(n) territory.
neetcode.Stack: Anything about matching, nesting, or “the most recent unmatched thing” is a stack in disguise — parentheses validation and calculator-style expression evaluation are the canonical shapes.
neetcode.Binary Search: The hard part is rarely the search itself — it's proving the search space is monotonic (sorted, or has a “yes below this point, no above it” boundary) before you binary search over it at all.
neetcode.Linked List: Draw the pointers on paper before writing code. Fast/slow pointers and dummy head nodes resolve nearly every 'reverse', 'find the middle', or 'detect a cycle' variant.
neetcode.Trees: Almost every tree problem is a traversal (DFS or BFS) with one extra piece of state threaded through — the skill is picking the right traversal and knowing whether that extra state flows down (as a parameter) or up (as a return value).
neetcode.Heap / Priority Queue: Reach for a heap the moment a problem asks for the “k best/smallest/largest” repeatedly — a fixed-size heap that evicts its worst element is almost always faster than re-sorting.
neetcode.Backtracking: Backtracking is DFS over a decision tree with an explicit undo step: make a choice, recurse, then revert it. The undo is what people forget, and it's the actual difference between backtracking and plain recursion.
neetcode.Tries: A trie trades memory for prefix speed — use it the moment a problem needs “does any word start with this prefix” answered repeatedly, since that's a walk down one path rather than a scan of every word.
neetcode.Graphs: Build the adjacency list first, then decide BFS vs. DFS: BFS for shortest paths in unweighted graphs, DFS when you only care about reachability, cycles, or ordering.
neetcode.Advanced Graphs: This tier is about graph algorithms with an extra constraint layered on top — weighted shortest paths, ordering with dependencies — where the base BFS/DFS gets replaced by Dijkstra, topological sort, or Union-Find depending on what the constraint actually is.
neetcode.1-D Dynamic Programming: Define what a single index represents in the recurrence before writing any code — once state(i) is defined in words, the transition is usually a short formula in terms of state(i-1) and state(i-2).
neetcode.2-D Dynamic Programming: Two-dimensional DP almost always means two sequences (or one sequence and one constraint) being compared position by position — sketch the table by hand for a tiny input before generalizing the recurrence.
neetcode.Greedy: Greedy only works when you can prove the locally-best choice never costs you later — when in doubt, look for a sorting order (by end time, ratio, or deadline) that makes the greedy choice obviously safe.
neetcode.Intervals: Sort by start (or end) time first — nearly every interval problem becomes a single linear pass once the intervals are in the right order.
neetcode.Math & Geometry: These test careful index manipulation more than deep math — rotating a matrix or walking it in a spiral is about precisely tracking boundaries, not about a formula you're missing.
neetcode.Bit Manipulation: XOR's self-cancelling property, shifting to check/set/clear a bit, and counting set bits cover almost everything in this category — the hard part is recognizing when a problem is secretly about bits at all.
